video.title: Training and testing: Hold some data back
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Ms Salma - the students' geography teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Last year I built a model to predict which pupils would pass. On last year's pupils it was right every time. This year it was wrong for one pupil in three.
Today: why we test a model on data it has never seen.
The fix is simple. Split your data before you start: about eighty percent to train the model, and twenty percent locked away to test it. The test set plays the part of next year's pupils.
A model can remember its training pupils without learning anything useful. The test pupils are new to it, so its score on them is an honest guess of how it will do next year.

scenes.on_screen_text: Errors as the model gets more complex
scenes.narration: Here is the test error as we make the model more and more complex. It falls at first, then rises again. The middle model is the best one for new pupils.
A model that bends to fit every training pupil is overfitting. It learns the noise, like one pupil's lucky day, as if it were a rule. It looks perfect in training and fails on new data.
One rule matters most. Never peek at the test set while you build the model. If you tune the model to the test pupils, the test stops being fair.
Quick check! A model scores one hundred percent on its training pupils and sixty percent on the test pupils. Which score tells you how it will do next year?
The test score, sixty percent. The perfect training score only shows the model remembered its pupils. The big gap is a sign of overfitting.
In the app, open the overfitting lab. Raise the complexity slider and watch the training error fall while the test error turns back up.
Your turn. Why do we keep twenty percent of the data away from the model while we build it?
To check it on pupils it has never seen. Remember: train on most of the data, test once on the rest, and a big gap between the two scores means overfitting.
Try it yourself: make a rule from ten cards, then test it on five hidden cards. Did your rule still work on the cards it had never seen?
